title: A "CSV" from a European Excel is delimited with semicolons, and a comma-delimiter parser reads the whole line as one field
assumption: A file with a .csv extension is comma-delimited.

input.description: A CSV exported by Excel configured for a locale (most of continental Europe) where the decimal comma is the default decimal separator - Excel then uses a semicolon as the list/field separator instead of a comma, to avoid colliding with decimal commas in numeric fields, while still naming the file .csv.

what_goes_wrong: Parsing this file with a comma-delimited reader produces one single-column row per line - `['name;age']`, `['Ada;30']` - instead of the two columns the file actually has; every downstream column lookup by index or name silently gets the wrong (and only) field.
why: ".csv" names a family of delimited-text formats, not a guarantee of which character is the delimiter. When Excel on Windows saves as CSV it uses the operating system's regional "list separator" setting, and in locales whose decimal separator is a comma (most of continental Europe) that setting defaults to a semicolon, so numbers like 3,5 don't collide with the field separator. The file still gets the same ".csv" extension. A parser that hardcodes `delimiter=","` has no way to detect this from the extension alone.

repros.code:
import csv, io
text = 'name;age\nAda;30\n'
print(list(csv.reader(io.StringIO(text))))
print(list(csv.reader(io.StringIO(text), delimiter=";")))

fix: Sniff the delimiter instead of hardcoding it - Python's `csv.Sniffer().sniff(sample)` guesses it from a sample of the file, or check the first line for the most frequent of `,`, `;`, and `\t` before choosing a reader. Let users confirm the detected delimiter on upload rather than failing silently.

sources.title: RFC 4180: Common Format and MIME Type for Comma-Separated Values (CSV) Files

test_cases.note: A CSV-parsing function that auto-detects the delimiter should return two columns for this semicolon-delimited file, not one column containing the whole line.
